step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Inventory: the whiteboard shows a pathologist/doctor icon, a hospital icon, EKS, two S3 buckets (input images and model output), SageMaker, FSx and IAM. The two S3 buckets do different jobs (raw image ingestion vs. model/result storage), so they stay separate nodes. 2) Flow from the transcript: hospitals, biologists and clients send medical images to S3 (about 5 TB per project); the images are loaded into the Kubernetes (EKS) product, which is a labelling platform; pathologists annotate and label the data; the enriched data is used to train one model per project in SageMaker, using the same Docker containers as before; SageMaker trains with FSx (IO performance) and IAM (security and data control); the model is saved in an S3 bucket; the model and results are exported back to the EKS product, where the pathologist validates or rejects it; once validated the model is frozen and moved to inference on the same Kubernetes platform, used by hospitals. 3) Edges follow the drawn arrows. The FSx and IAM lines to SageMaker have no arrowheads on the board, so their direction follows the world model (FSx to SageMaker as data, IAM to SageMaker as control). 4) The pathologist is typed as UserCompanyDomainExpert rather than the world model's UserConsumerWeb, because the icon is a doctor and the transcript describes an expert annotator. 5) Hospital use of the validated model for inference is spoken but not drawn as an arrow, so it is recorded in notes only. 6) Metrics (5 TB per project, training more than 30x faster, up to 30% infrastructure cost savings, thousands of parallel trainings, HDS certification, regional data residency) are placed in notes.

graph.name: Kinaï (as transcribed): Medical Image Annotation and Per-Project ML Training on EKS and SageMaker
graph.notes: Healthcare company building technology for research and clinical studies, guiding pathologists and doctors in analysing medical images. Hospitals send images to S3 (about 5 TB per project); pathologists annotate them on an EKS-hosted labelling platform; SageMaker trains one model per project with FSx and IAM; models are stored in S3 and exported back to EKS for validation and then inference. Benefits: scientists work on several projects at once and switch in seconds, thousands of trainings in parallel, training more than 30x faster, up to 30% infrastructure cost savings (pay only when resources are used). Compliance: HDS certification and data kept in the project's region (e.g. Germany).

nodes.name: Hospital
nodes.notes: Hospitals, biologists and clients send medical images and data to S3. Hospitals later use the validated model for inference.

nodes.name: S3 (input images)
nodes.notes: Buckets receiving medical images from hospitals and clients; about 5 TB of data per project. Data is kept in the project's region (e.g. Germany).

nodes.name: EKS
nodes.notes: Kubernetes product: labelling platform where pathologists annotate images, review model results and validate or reject models. Also hosts inference once a model is validated and frozen.

nodes.name: Pathologist
nodes.notes: Pathologist or doctor who enriches data by annotating and labelling images, and validates or rejects the trained model.

nodes.name: Amazon SageMaker
nodes.notes: Trains one model per project using the same Docker containers as the previous pipelines, which made migration easy. Thousands of trainings in parallel, more than 30x faster, up to 30% infrastructure cost savings.

nodes.name: Amazon FSx
nodes.notes: File system used with SageMaker training for IO performance.

nodes.name: IAM
nodes.notes: Security and fine-grained control of data access; helps document and meet medical certifications.

nodes.name: S3 (models)
nodes.notes: Bucket where the trained model and results are saved. HDS certification demonstrates health data security.
